name: Green tea / EGCG
lead: Green tea is steamed or pan-fired tea made from Camellia sinensis leaves, and its main catechin, epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), is sold as a concentrated extract. People use green tea and its extracts as a mild thermogenic or fat-loss support: the idea is a small lift in energy expenditure and fat oxidation that adds to training and a calorie deficit, producing a leaner look. Dried green tea leaves contain about 7,380 mg of EGCG per 100 g, far more than black tea.[1]

The tea has a long history in China and Japan, where it was drunk as a daily beverage and, from the early thirteenth century, promoted as medicine.[13] Matcha, the powdered shade-grown form, spread through Western cafes and social media in the 2000s and 2010s.[14] Published research ranges from cell and mouse studies to randomised trials: a 2024 meta-analysis of 59 trials reported small reductions in body mass, BMI and body fat percentage with green tea extract, and a smaller trial program has looked at fat oxidation during exercise.[16][17]

Regulators have raised safety concerns about concentrated extracts: the European Food Safety Authority stated in 2018 that daily intakes of 800 mg or more of EGCG could increase the risk of liver damage, and Wikipedia's supplement overview lists green tea catechins among the ingredients most implicated in supplement-related liver injury.[1][3] Brewed tea is considered safe by EFSA when traditionally prepared.[13]

angle.text: Green tea and EGCG are used as a gentle fat-loss support. Proponents describe a small metabolic lift that adds to diet and training; trials report small changes in body mass and body fat percentage.

infobox: Sold as a dietary supplement; FDA warning letters issued over disease claims

paras: People take green tea and concentrated green tea extract for body composition: the stated chain is a mild increase in energy expenditure and fat oxidation, a small contribution to a calorie deficit, and a leaner look as body fat falls. Green tea is also an ingredient in many fat-burner products and a common drink among people cutting weight. Green tea catechins have been examined in laboratory work on inflammation,[4] and a 2024 systematic review of topical cosmeceuticals for photoaging included green tea among the botanicals it searched.[23]

Matcha, the powdered, shade-grown form of green tea, is drunk whole rather than steeped, so the drinker consumes the leaf itself. Wikipedia reports that matcha spread in the United States from Japanese grocers through health-food retailers in the early 2000s and then through Instagram and TikTok, and that Starbucks and Dunkin' added matcha drinks.[14]
Green tea and EGCG have been studied for conditions including acne, obesity with high LDL, diabetes and cancer prevention, listed under Clinical studies below.[7][8][9]

Green tea is made from Camellia sinensis leaves and buds that are not withered or oxidised, and it originated in China in the late first millennium BC according to Wikipedia. Lu Yu wrote The Classic of Tea between 618 and 907 AD, and tea seeds reached Japan in the early ninth century.[13] Chinese green tea was originally steamed and, after the early Ming dynasty, mostly pan-fired in a wok, while Japan still mainly steams, giving a sweeter, grassier taste.[13]

In Japan the monk Eisai brought the powdered-tea method from China in the late twelfth century, and his 1211 text Kissa Yojoki, presented to the shogun in 1214, framed tea as a form of medicine.[13][14] That medicinal framing continues in modern marketing of tea extracts. About 1.7 million tonnes of green tea were produced in 2013, with China supplying about 80 percent of the market in 2015.[13]

The modern supplement form dates to extraction of concentrated catechins. In 2006 the FDA approved a green tea extract ointment for genital warts, per Wikipedia, which is a separate use from the oral supplements.[13]

Epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) is the most abundant catechin in tea, a polyphenol formed from epigallocatechin and gallic acid. Dried green tea leaves contain about 7,380 mg per 100 g, far more than black tea, in which most catechins are converted during processing.[1] Brewed green tea has about 12 mg of caffeine per 100 g, and extracts may reach up to 17.4 percent caffeine by weight.[13]

Shading changes the profile. Wikipedia says matcha's shading for two to three weeks before harvest increases chlorophyll, caffeine and free amino acids such as theanine while reducing catechin accumulation.[14]

EGCG is mainly absorbed in the intestine, and gut bacteria play a role in its metabolism before absorption.[2] Oral bioavailability is poor even at intakes equivalent to 8 to 16 cups of green tea daily, which can cause nausea or heartburn. Blood levels peak after about 1.7 hours, and methylated metabolites can reach 8 to 25 times the plasma level of unmetabolised EGCG.[1]

Laboratory studies report a range of effects, including anti-inflammatory activity and effects on cancer cell lines such as melanoma.[4][5][6] A 2022 review in Molecules describes antioxidant, hypoglycaemic and other pharmacological activities of green tea and also raises hepatotoxicity concerns for extracts.[21] These are mainly cell and animal findings. A mouse study reported lower body weight and altered gene expression in adipose tissue with EGCG in diet-induced obese mice.[12]

A 2011 European Food Safety Authority analysis found no demonstrated cause-and-effect link between tea catechins and maintaining normal LDL cholesterol; a 2016 systematic review by Momose and colleagues found small LDL reductions at high doses over 4 to 14 weeks.[1] Wikipedia's green tea article summarises a 2013 Cochrane meta-analysis of trials longer than three months as finding lower total and LDL cholesterol, small blood pressure drops of about 2 to 3 mm Hg, and weak or inconclusive evidence for cancer and cardiovascular benefit, and says no good evidence supports weight loss.[13]

Trials on body composition give mixed pictures. In a 12-week randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 102 women with central obesity taking 856.8 mg per day of green tea extract, weight in the treatment group fell from 76.8 to 75.7 kg, with reductions in BMI, waist circumference and total cholesterol and changes in ghrelin and adiponectin; the authors reported no adverse events.[15] A 2024 dose-response meta-analysis of 59 randomised trials with 3,802 participants reported that body mass, body fat percentage and BMI decreased with green tea extract, while fat mass, leptin and ghrelin were not significantly affected; certainty ranged from low to high.[16]

Exercise studies are small. In a randomised crossover trial of 13 women, matcha drinks before a 30-minute brisk walk lowered respiratory exchange ratio and raised fat oxidation from 0.31 to 0.35 g per minute, and the authors cautioned the effect should not be overstated in weight-loss programmes.[17] In a trial in untrained men, matcha taken twice daily during 8 or 12 weeks of resistance training was associated with a larger gain in skeletal muscle mass in the 12-week trial, lower salivary cortisol and lower post-exercise fatigue.[18]

A 2018 review by Hu and colleagues found that excessive EGCG intake may cause liver toxicity, and considered 338 mg per day safe as a capsule or tablet and 704 mg per day safe as a tea beverage. EFSA estimates a cup of green tea contains about 165 mg of EGCG.[1] Liver injury from weight-loss and bodybuilding supplements most often involves hepatocellular injury, with green tea catechins among the most implicated ingredients.[3][22]

Wikipedia reports that EFSA found raised liver enzymes with long-term intake above 800 mg EGCG per day, that EFSA considers traditionally prepared green tea safe, and that Health Canada recommended in 2017 a warning label and adult-only use for extracts.[13] A 2020 Cochrane review is described there as listing gastrointestinal problems, raised liver enzymes and rarely insomnia among extract side effects, and green tea interferes with the chemotherapy drug bortezomib and related proteasome inhibitors.[13]

From 2008 to 2017 the US FDA issued warning letters to EGCG supplement makers, mostly because promotional claims treated or prevented diseases, making the products unapproved new drugs under US law.[1]

On looksmax.org green tea comes up as a milder caffeine source. One poster who had cut caffeine said they planned a weekend cup of green tea, noting the belief that other compounds in the tea soften caffeine's effects; a reply said a mug before bed helps them sleep despite the caffeine.[19] Another thread proposes green tea extract with quercetin and a levodopa-containing herb as a way to raise dopamine, reasoning that catechins and quercetin inhibit enzymes that break down dopamine; replies there recommended other compounds instead.[20] These are forum opinions, not trial results.

Registered human trials of green tea extract or EGCG include a trial in women with acne (NCT01846338, n=80, status unknown),[7] a phase 3 trial in obese women with high LDL (NCT02116517, n=73),[8] a phase 3 trial in type 2 diabetes with hyperlipidemia (NCT01360567, n=102),[9] and trials in colorectal cancer chemoprevention, endometriosis, uterine fibroids, endothelial function, diabetic nephropathy, hepatitis C and asthma.[10][11] The registry entries do not report results, so they are not evidence of effect.

Published randomised trials on weight and body composition are described under Effectiveness.[15][16] A 12-month randomised trial of matcha in older adults with cognitive decline examined cognition and sleep rather than appearance.[25] Animal work includes a study in which EGCG reduced body weight in diet-induced obese mice,[12] which is not a human trial.

lore.intro: Green tea is discussed in looksmaxxing and fitness forums as a mild caffeine source and fat-loss helper, and occasionally as part of dopamine or focus stacks.[19][20]

claims.claim: Green tea extract is a mild fat burner
claims.believers: Supplement marketers and some lifters say EGCG with caffeine nudges energy expenditure and fat oxidation, helping a cut.[17]
claims.experts: A 2024 meta-analysis of 59 trials reported small reductions in body mass and body fat percentage, with fat mass unchanged; Wikipedia's green tea article says no good evidence supports weight loss.[16][13]

claims.claim: Green tea's caffeine is gentler than coffee, so it can be drunk late in the day
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster said other compounds in the tea soften caffeine's effects, and a reply said a mug before bed helps them sleep.[19]
claims.experts: A systematic review examines the cognitive effects of caffeine combined with L-theanine, an amino acid found in tea, and Wikipedia reports brewed green tea has about 12 mg caffeine per 100 g and extracts can contain much more, and rare insomnia is listed among extract side effects.[24][13]

claims.claim: Catechins and quercetin can raise dopamine
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread argues catechins and quercetin inhibit enzymes (DDC, COMT, MAO) involved in dopamine breakdown and proposes combining them with a levodopa-containing herb.[20]
claims.experts: No published human trials were found testing this combination for dopamine or mood.

claims.believers: Proponents of high-dose extracts point to trials such as one using 856.8 mg per day in obese women, which reported small weight reductions.[15]
claims.experts: EFSA stated in 2018 that 800 mg or more of EGCG daily could raise liver-damage risk, and Hu and colleagues considered 338 mg per day safe as capsules.[1]

claims.believers: Proponents point to matcha's catechins, amino acids and fibre as the reason it might support recovery and training adaptation.[18]
claims.experts: A trial in untrained men reported a larger muscle-mass gain and lower cortisol with matcha during 12 weeks of resistance training; the authors conclude daily matcha may support muscle adaptation.[18]

claims.believers: Tea drinkers cite lowered LDL as a metabolic benefit.[13]
claims.experts: A 2011 EFSA analysis found no demonstrated link; a 2013 Cochrane meta-analysis summarised on Wikipedia found lower total and LDL cholesterol in longer trials.[1][13]

card.summary: Green tea catechin sold as a mild fat-burner; mostly lab and animal evidence, with liver-safety warnings for concentrated extracts.
card.note: EFSA says 800 mg or more of EGCG daily could raise liver-damage risk.

quick.overview:
Green tea and its main catechin, EGCG, are taken as a gentle thermogenic for fat loss, either as tea or as concentrated capsule extracts.
Most published work on EGCG is laboratory or animal research, and no completed human trial has shown an appearance effect.
quick.mechanism: EGCG is absorbed in the intestine and metabolised with help from gut bacteria; oral absorption is poor. Cell and mouse studies report anti-inflammatory and metabolic effects, which have not been established in people for appearance.
quick.risks: EFSA stated in 2018 that 800 mg or more of EGCG daily could increase liver-damage risk, and green tea catechins are among the ingredients most implicated in supplement-related liver injury. The FDA has sent warning letters to EGCG makers over disease claims.
